segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The origin of the term "Bollywood" - combining the Hindi-language film industry of the former Bombay with "Hollywood" - dates back to the 1970s. Many of its stars - among them the biggest of all, Amitabh Bachchan (b. 1942) - reject the term, preferring to replace it with "Indian film industry". But Bachchan is wrong. Although in the West "Bollywood" is synonymous with Indian cinema, in reality it is only a fraction of the vast ocean that makes up the Indian film industry.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Bollywood produces only a quarter of the nearly one thousand films made in the country each year. The South Indian film industry (an area covering the Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, and Kannada languages) accounts for more than 75% of Indian productions and their revenue, according to a 2009 Ernst & Young report, with Tamil and Telugu output rivaling that of Bollywood. In any case, although Bombay has become Mumbai, and bearing in mind that Hindi cinema, though produced in the national language, is not representative of the country as a whole, Bollywood remains its most visible and celebrated export. Today, Bollywood films are more accessible to international audiences than they were 10 years ago, thanks to their appeal to different cultures beyond the Indian diaspora.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: During the 2000s, the Hindi film industry moved away from the romantic musical melodramas and bloody revenge dramas characteristic of the two previous decades. Some of the decade's biggest hits were non-resident Indian (NRI) romances, films whose protagonists lived in foreign cities such as London or New York but held on to Indian moral values. These films, dear to first-generation immigrants living in the United Kingdom and the United States, owed their box office success both to the domestic market and to NRI viewers, who paid for their tickets in dollars and pounds.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Although films were increasingly set in India, audiences' thirst for foreign settings, first quenched by Raj Kapoor (1924-1988) in Sangam (1964), led many of the decade's hits to include at least a few musical numbers staged in another part of the world. The two biggest hits of 2000, Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai (2000) and Mohabbatein (2000), feature many scenes shot outside India.

The two biggest hits of two thousand, Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai, from two thousand, and Mohabbatein, from two thousand, feature many scenes shot outside India.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The former, a commercial film with a run-of-the-mill theme and plenty of song and dance, was shot mainly in New Zealand by director Rakesh Roshan (b. 1949), a former actor who introduced his son Hrithik Roshan as a viable heroic alternative in an industry dominated by the Khans - Shah Rukh, Aamir, and Salman. Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai was also responsible for turning New Zealand into a tourist destination for affluent Indians, something veteran director and producer Yash Chopra (b. 1932) had managed to do for Switzerland by using the country as a location for several films since the 1970s. Unusually for Bollywood films, Mohabbatein, directed by Chopra's son Aditya (b. 1970), is set entirely in a school (in India, but shot in the United Kingdom), and for the first time brought together superstar Shah Rukh Khan as a champion of young lovers who stands up to a strict headmaster, played by the superstar of the previous generation, Amitabh Bachchan. The pair appeared throughout the decade in a series of hits, in particular Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham, in which Khan plays a rebellious son who stands up to his strict father, played by Bachchan.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The following year saw the release of several films that would hugely influence Bollywood over the next decade. A four-hour epic about cricket set in the British colonial period of the 1890s, Lagaan: Once Upon a Time in India (2001) initially failed to attract any backers. Films about cricket had not done well at the box office, despite the sport's immense popularity on the subcontinent. Finally, Aamir Khan, the film's star, decided to take a chance and produce it himself. The picture, directed by Ashutosh Gowariker (b. 1964), became a colossal hit and earned an Oscar nomination for Best Foreign Language Film.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The lesson Aamir Khan, a famous heartthrob throughout the 1990s, learned from Lagaan: Once Upon a Time in India was to choose fewer films to act in, opting only for those with themes that broke away from the usual Bollywood formula, and to produce singular works. His new mantra resulted in films such as 3 Idiots (2009), directed by Rajkumar Hirani (b. 1962), which questioned the Indian education system and became Bollywood's biggest box office record-holder of all time; the film he directed himself, Taare Zameen Par (Like Stars on Earth, 2007), which dealt with dyslexia; Rang De Basanti (2006), by Rakeysh Mehra (b. 1963), centered on the discontent of young Indians; and the debut of Anusha Rizvi (b. 1978), PEEPLI [Live] (2010), which took jabs at India's byte-hungry electronic media while highlighting the endemic problem of farmer suicides in the country. The film became a box office hit without Khan or any other well-known star in front of the camera.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Dil Chahta Hai (2001), directed by Farhan Akhtar (b. 1974) and starring Aamir Khan and Saif Ali Khan, was also released in 2001. The film revolves around the lives of three friends and was notable for being the first to openly target an urban audience. Previously, Bollywood had made "pan-Indian" films, with something for everyone, from the well-off executive to the housewife and the taxi driver. Akhtar recognized that the bulk of revenue would be generated by the booming urban multiplex culture, in which people pay much higher ticket prices to sit in air-conditioned comfort and watch films about people like themselves. This paved the way for a boom in urban-themed productions and inevitably led to the rise of young directors who had different stories to tell and did not rely on preconceived formulas.

segments.original: At the forefront of this movement were directors such as Anurag Kashyap (b. 1972) and Dibakar Banerjee (b. 1969) who, despite working within the Bollywood system, told staggeringly different stories made on micro-budgets. Banerjee's debut film, Khosla Ka Ghosla! (2006), was about an ordinary family dealing with Delhi land grabbers, while LSD: Love, Sex aur Dhokha (2010) explored the emotions of love, sex, and betrayal as seen through handheld cameras, spy cams, mobile cameras, and security cameras. Kashyap's Dev.D (2009) takes the classic love-triangle novel Devdas, adapted for the screen many times, and turns it into a sex- and drug-fueled descent into hell.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The usual melodramas and action films continued to be made in Bollywood. Shah Rukh Khan appeared in several of them, such as Main Hoon Na (2004), Veer-Zaara (2004), and Kabhi Alvida Naa Kehna (2006), cementing his status as a superstar. Audiences, however, rejected him when he tried to play different characters in films such as Aśoka (2001) and Paheli (2005). The former, directed by Santosh Sivan (b. 1961), is a largely fictional historical drama about the life of the ancient Indian emperor Ashoka the Great (Khan), who converted to Buddhism. Xenophobia also seemed alive and well in the hero played by Sunny Deol, spouting slogans and taking on the entire Pakistani Army to rescue his kidnapped wife and son in Gadar: Ek Prem Katha (2001).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The 2000s saw strong growth in Bollywood comedies aimed at India's large young population. However, Akshay Kumar's transformation from action hero into a major comedy star took the industry by surprise. He appeared in a string of broad, rowdy comedies that threw in everything from the films of previous decades. Namastey London (2007), Heyy Babyy (2007), and Housefull (2010) were colossal hits, proving that a significant market for the old Bollywood style still exists.
